reading.ours: two units of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — an instrument check, and it is printed first because nothing below it means anything until it passes. The true ratio is a little UNDER 2: both sides pay the driving loop once, so the exact expectation is (2u + L) / (u + L) with L the loop and u one unit, which at sixteen dependent steps per unit puts it around 1.9. A reading below 1.5 means this process could not resolve a deliberate doubling, and the runner voids the report rather than printing prices under it.

reading.ours: one unit of arithmetic per iteration
reading.floor: the same body again, over its own copy of the same state
reading.caveat: NOT A PRICE — the noise floor. The two sides are identical code over identical, separately-allocated state, so the true ratio is 1.00 exactly and every departure from it printed here was produced by this machine at this moment. The rule that follows is the one the whole table is read under: NO RATIO CLOSER TO 1.00 THAN THIS GAP IS A READING. It also bounds the per-row noise figure, which is the same idea measured again inside every pair — each pair times its floor twice, once before our side and once after, and prints how far the two disagreed.

reading.ours: collection.upsert(row) — a key this population has never seen
reading.caveat: THE FLOOR DOES LESS, AND KNOWABLY SO. Ours mints an identity (a sixteen-field slot, a links cell per index, an entry in the identity store), copies the row, walks the copy's own names to refuse the ones a row may not carry, stamps the slot, stamps the collection and records the row on the presence channel so every index and every whole-population reader hears about it. The floor allocates one copy and hashes one string. Direction: this inflates our ratio, and no three-line floor can close the gap — what the extra buys is that anything subscribed to this population, or indexing it, is woken by this insert. The tracked row below is the closest a few lines get. Both sides abandon their container between passes and both are collected outside the clock, so the GC of what each allocated is NOT inside either number; our allocation per row is roughly three objects to the floor's one, and that debt is paid later.

reading.ours: collection.upsert(row) — a key this population has never seen
reading.floor: map.set(id, copy) into a store that also queues what changed
reading.caveat: THE FAIRER FLOOR, and it is still not equal. The floor now keeps a per-row frame stamp and a queue, so something downstream could be told — which is the job our insert is doing and the bare Map is not. What the floor still does not have: an identity that outlives the value, a per-index cell on every row, a presence channel that tells indexes and whole-population readers separately from the row itself, or any means of recording WHICH columns moved. Direction: still inflates our ratio, by less than the bare-Map row above. The pair of ratios brackets the truth; neither number alone is it.

reading.ours: collection.update(slot, patch) — one column, no index reads it
reading.caveat: THE LOOKUP IS ON NEITHER SIDE — ours holds the slot, the floor holds the object, both resolved outside the clock. That is the comparison this row is for. What ours does that a store cannot: it walks the patch, refuses names a row may not carry, gates each column on ===, builds the list of what moved, stamps the slot and the collection, and asks the dependents map for each moved column so an index could be routed. Direction: inflates our ratio; the tracked row below prices the part of that a person would have had to write anyway. The patch object is REUSED rather than written as a literal per call — a caller who writes { title } inline pays one more allocation per write than this row charges us for. The batch closes with one flush per eight thousand writes, which is why every write in it takes the marking path rather than the already-stamped early return.

reading.ours: collection.update(slot, patch) — one column, no index reads it
reading.floor: gate on !==, stamp the row once per frame, queue it, store
reading.caveat: THE FLOOR NOW DOES THE JOB. It compares before it writes, so a re-send moves nothing; it stamps the row with the frame number so ten writes to one row queue it once; and it queues the row so a frame could deliver it. Four lines. What it still does not do: record WHICH columns moved (so no field-granular subscription is possible), route to an index, or mark the collection separately from the row. Direction: still inflates our ratio, and this is the number to quote when somebody asks what the engine costs over doing it properly by hand.

reading.ours: collection.update(slot, patch) with the value the row already holds
reading.floor: row.title = value — a store that always happens
reading.caveat: THE TWO SIDES DO OPPOSITE THINGS, ON PURPOSE. Ours walks the patch, finds every column equal, returns before marking anything and wakes nobody; the floor stores unconditionally because it has nothing to protect. So this is not "which is faster at the same work" — it is what the comparator gate costs when it fires, against the cheapest possible thing that ignores the question. No flush closes this batch, because nothing was marked and there is nothing for a frame to deliver: that is the point of the row. Direction: inflates our ratio; what the gate buys is that a screen re-sending a server payload it already holds does not repaint.

reading.floor: const row = map.get(id); if (row !== undefined) row.title = value
reading.caveat: THE ONE WRITE ROW WHERE BOTH SIDES PAY THE LOOKUP, which is what makes it the fair comparison for a key that arrived from outside. Ours is one map read and then the identity path priced two rows up; the floor is one map read and a store. The difference between this ratio and the update.column ratio is the price of NOT having held the identity — the engine's own source puts that at 103-132 ns against 36-51, and this row is the independent check on that claim.

reading.ours: collection.upsert(row) — a key that already carries a value
reading.floor: copy five columns onto the stored object, one store each
reading.caveat: THE FLOOR CANNOT EXPRESS ONE HALF OF WHAT UPSERT PROMISES. An upsert of an existing key also REMOVES the columns the new value does not carry, which means walking the stored row to find them; here both rows carry all five columns, so that walk finds nothing and the floor's five stores are the same net effect. Ours additionally gates each column on ===, so only the column that actually moved is written and reported, where the floor writes all five every time. Direction: mixed — the gate saves us four stores and costs us five comparisons plus a moved-list allocation, and the marking and routing are ours alone. Read it beside update.column: the difference between the two is what sending a whole row costs over sending the column that changed.

reading.ours: collection.update(slot, { group }) with one index over `group`
reading.floor: delete from the old Set, store the column, add to the new Set
reading.caveat: THE CLOSEST TO EQUAL WORK IN THIS SUITE, and the caveats are about WHEN rather than whether. Both sides move a row between two unordered groups, and both keep an empty group's container. Ours defers the actual filing to the frame drain, so the flush that closes the batch is where the membership moves — it is inside the timed body and is charged here. Ours additionally: records the row on the column's channel so every index reading `group` is offered it once, stamps both buckets so their subscribers can be woken, and keeps each bucket as a hold-counted identity that can be resolved by address. The floor can be read by iterating it and by nothing else. Direction: inflates our ratio, and what it buys is the only thing on this row that a screen actually needs — a list that repaints itself.

reading.ours: collection.remove(slot) — through the identity, no index registered
reading.caveat: THE HASH IS ON THE FLOOR'S SIDE ONLY: ours is handed the identity and the floor hashes a string, which flatters us — the removeByKey path is not priced here and would cost us that lookup too. Against that, ours does not free anything at the call: the identity outlives the value, subscribers stay, and the slot is offered to the frame's sweep to be released only if nothing holds it. The flush that closes the batch is where that sweep runs and it is inside the timed body. The floor's row is gone the instant delete returns and nothing can be subscribed to it. Both sides rebuild their population between passes, untimed.

reading.floor: map.delete(id) and Set.delete(row) from the group it was in
reading.caveat: Ours lets go of the membership through the cell the row already carries — no lookup of any kind — where the floor hashes the id and then hashes the group name. That flatters us and is the design being priced: the row knows where it is filed. Against that, ours stamps the bucket so its subscribers are woken, and offers both the row's identity and any bucket left empty to the frame's sweep, which runs inside the flush that closes this batch. The floor leaves an empty Set behind for ever and tells nobody.
